passage: Looking back, I nearly put Sahil's name in a complaint to our manager. Three weeks of reports had come back with the wrong columns, and I was quietly furious. I'm Keerthana, I was twenty-five, and it was my first time guiding someone. Before sending anything I asked myself: had I ever shown him a finished report? No. I had sent a two-line instruction and walked off. So I sat with him for an hour, opened last month's report, and marked each column: this one, from this sheet, like so. I watched him do the next one himself, then set a check-in for Friday. The Friday report was mostly right, with two small errors. It wasn't quick, but it also wasn't a story about a lazy junior. It was a story about my instructions.

qa.q: What had Keerthana given Sahil before the reports came back wrong?
qa.a: A two-line instruction, without showing him a finished report.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana stop before putting Sahil's name in the complaint?
qa.a: Though quietly furious, Keerthana wanted to be fair, asked whether Sahil had ever been shown a finished report, and realised the instructions might be the cause.

qa.q: What could Keerthana do if the reports still came back wrong after several coaching sessions?
qa.a: Keerthana could talk openly with Sahil about the remaining gaps, then bring the manager in with a clear record of what had already been tried. 🙂

qa.q: How might Sahil have felt during the hour at his desk?
qa.a: He may have felt relieved that expectations became clear, with a model to follow, though perhaps a little embarrassed too.

grounding: Shows a senior colleague clarifying expectations, giving an example, coaching and following up before blaming a junior.

passage:
Operations note, review of team lead Tenzin's handling of Ira's first month.

Ira's delivery schedules had errors three weeks running. Several of us expected Tenzin to escalate. Instead, on Monday, Tenzin sat with Ira and asked her to walk through how she built a schedule. It turned out the template she'd been given still used last year's warehouse codes. That explained half the errors.

Tenzin fixed the template first. Then Tenzin wrote down exactly what a correct schedule looks like, with two past examples, and sat beside Ira while she made the next one. Ira asked more questions in that hour than in the whole month.

On Friday Tenzin checked her schedule again. One small error, which she caught herself.

Tenzin told me, "If it had gone on after all this, I'd have raised it formally. But first I had to be sure the problem was her and not our system." I have recommended this approach to the other leads.

qa.q: What was wrong with the template Ira had been given?
qa.a: The template still used last year's warehouse codes.

qa.q: What was Ira probably feeling during the hour Tenzin sat beside her?
qa.a: Ira probably felt relieved and more confident, as she asked more questions in that hour than in the whole month.

qa.q: Which steps did Tenzin take before thinking about escalation, and why do they matter?
qa.a: Tenzin checked the system, fixed the template, gave clear examples, coached Ira and followed up; this makes sure a person isn't blamed for a system problem.

qa.q: How might the other leads see Tenzin's approach?
qa.a: Some had expected escalation, so they might be surprised, but the note-writer is recommending it to them as a better way.

grounding: Shows a team lead clarifying expectations, giving examples, coaching and following up with a junior, and checking the system before blaming the person.

passage:
Wednesday, late.

Irawati's invoices went out wrong again today. Third time this month. The client emailed my boss, and my boss emailed me with one line: "Manoj, sort this out."

My first thought was to write her up. My second was to just do the invoices myself. I did neither.

At five I sat with her and asked her to show me her process. She pulled up the training document, and there it was: the tax step was in the old order. She had followed it exactly. Nobody had updated it.

I felt stupid and a bit relieved. I rewrote that page with her, gave her two correct invoices as examples, and said, "Friday we check together, then Monday you do them alone, and I review."

She said, "Thank you. I thought I was just bad at this."

If it's still wrong after two weeks of this, then we'll have a harder talk. Not before.

qa.q: What was wrong in the training document?
qa.a: The tax step was in the old order.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling on discovering the training document was wrong?
qa.a: Manoj felt foolish and a bit relieved, realising the errors came from the system rather than from Irawati's carelessness.

qa.q: What plan did Manoj make, and why is it fair?
qa.a: Fixing the document, giving examples, checking together on Friday and reviewing on Monday before any escalation; it gives Irawati a real chance after the system is fixed.

qa.q: How was Irawati seeing herself before Manoj sat with her?
qa.a: Irawati thought she was just bad at the work, which likely made her feel discouraged and anxious.

grounding: Shows a manager who checks the system, clarifies expectations, gives examples and follows up with a junior before escalating.
